title: The Bus Station
strapline: All aboard! Tickets please, ding the bell, and mind the doors — journeys with a driver in charge.
intent: A bus is a shared journey children know from real life, and role-playing it lets them replay and make sense of travelling, waiting, paying and arriving.
Being the driver, conductor or passenger invites cooperative, turn-taking play with clear roles and a real sequence of stops.
Selling and checking tickets, counting fares and reading the route give number and print an urgent, genuine purpose.
Arranging chairs into a bus, steering and calling the stops is imaginative, physical work with plenty of room for planning.
The bus welcomes talk about where we're going, who's on board and how we get around — connecting to children's real neighbourhoods and journeys.
It naturally raises ideas of destinations, timetables, waiting your turn and looking after fellow passengers.
implementation: Set out rows of chairs, a steering wheel, a driver's seat and a bell, and let children build and rebuild the bus.
Add tickets, a ticket machine, coins and a route map with named stops so paying and navigating mean something.
Take on roles alongside them — a passenger who's lost, who's paying with the wrong coin — to stretch the talk and the problem-solving.
Count fares and passengers together: 'three getting on, how many tickets do you need?'
Name real local stops and destinations children know, and talk about journeys their families make.
If you can, take a real bus ride, then watch which words and routines the children carry into their play.
key_questions: Three getting on — how many tickets do you need?
Where is this bus going, and which stops will we make?
Ding! Who wants the next stop?
You've paid with the wrong coin — can you help me sort it out?
Who is driving, and who is the conductor today?

impact.text: Children take on roles as driver, conductor and passenger in cooperative, turn-taking play.
Children sell and check tickets and count fares and passengers, giving number a real purpose.
Children read the route and its stops, putting print to work.
Children talk about journeys their families make and where they are going.
Children build and rebuild the bus, planning and problem-solving together.

enhancements: A ticket machine, coins and a route map with named local stops children know.
Adult roles that stretch the play — a lost passenger, a wrong-coin fare.
A real bus ride, then watching which words and routines the children carry into their play.
A destinations board and a bell to call the stops.
Timetables and journey cards for mark-making with a purpose.

playing_exploring: Children build the bus and step into roles they know from real journeys, driving, paying and travelling.
The props — wheel, bell, tickets — pull children straight into the story.
active_learning: Running the route means holding several jobs at once — driving, stopping, selling tickets — and children stay with the busyness because it matters.
creating_thinking: Children invent routes, stops and solutions — what do we do when a passenger has no money, or wants a stop we've passed?
